{"summary":"Product brief — Native msw menu-bar monitor

Product principle: ship a monitor and launcher, not a graphical replacement for the CLI. The repository defines three fixed, isolated workspaces (dev, playgrounds, personal), each with its own VM, persistent workspace and Docker volumes, loopback IP, browser hostname, resource limits, and GitHub trust boundary. The app should make their state and frequent safe actions instantly visible while leaving credential, destructive, and parameter-heavy workflows in the terminal.

First-release experience: the menu-bar icon communicates aggregate state (all stopped, one or more running, action pending, or attention required). Its popover contains one row per workspace with name, running/stopped/error state, a compact CPU/memory indicator when available, and primary actions: Open Terminal, Open in Zed, Open Website, Start, Stop, and Restart. It also provides Refresh, Start All, Stop All with confirmation, Open Details, and Quit. Actions must show pending state, reject duplicates, refresh immediately on completion, and display an actionable error with the equivalent msw command.

Capability matrix:
P0/menu bar — aggregate and per-workspace state; start/stop/restart for one workspace; start/stop all; launch the workspace shell; open Zed; open a configured or recent published port; manual refresh; pending/error/stale indicators. These map to msw status, start, stop, restart, dev/playgrounds/personal, zed, open, and url.
P0/detail window — one page per workspace showing state, fixed hostname, configured CPU/memory allocation and ceiling, live CPU/memory metrics while the page is visible, recent action/error, and explicit lifecycle/launch controls. Include the published-port reference and copyable URL builder. Do not auto-run msw disk because that command calls ensure_running and would wake a stopped VM.
P1/detail window — on-demand disk and Docker usage; repository inventory with Open Terminal/Open Zed actions; GitHub credential presence without revealing tokens; bounded log preview; quick health check; favorite ports and recent projects; backup destination, last successful backup, and a foreground backup job with progress and completion notification. These map to disk, repos, github status, logs, check, ports, and backup. Advanced arguments remain available through a “Copy command” or “Open in Terminal” affordance.
P1/menu bar — optional sustained CPU/memory pressure badges, unexpected-stop and action-failure notifications, configurable favorite website shortcuts, and a concise last-backup status.
P2/detail window — rolling resource history, sustained disk alerts, managed temporary tunnels, repository fetch/pull status, update availability, and a command/activity history. Clone or pull may be reconsidered only if a safe typed workflow proves materially faster than opening a terminal.
P2/platform — discover workspaces dynamically instead of assuming the current dev/playgrounds/personal array, support third-party detail panels through versioned capabilities, and expose automation through App Intents.
Terminal-only — exec; clone and all repository mutations; pull; push, including --yes and --force-with-lease; identity; GitHub setup/verify/remove; restore; resize; clean and --volumes; guest upgrade; MicroSandbox update; deep check; host repair; arbitrary log options; installer repair modes; docs/help/version. Push must remain terminal-only because the repository deliberately requires review of repository, branch, commit, and commits before the explicit host-only push path; restore replaces managed state and leaves every VM stopped; cleanup can delete unused Docker volumes; GitHub operations mutate Keychain-held credentials and can quarantine a workspace. Tunnels remain terminal-only in P0/P1 because their lifetime is tied to a foreground SSH process.

User stories:
1. As the owner, I can glance at one icon and know whether any workspace is running or needs attention.
2. I can start a stopped workspace and enter it in Ghostty or Zed without remembering a command; these launch paths may auto-start exactly as the CLI does.
3. I can open port 3000 in any workspace without confusing hosts, because each uses its documented dev.msw.test, playgrounds.msw.test, or personal.msw.test address.
4. I can stop an idle workspace or restart a failed one and see the confirmed resulting state.
5. I can inspect live resource pressure without keeping msw metrics --watch in a terminal.
6. I can diagnose an error from a bounded log excerpt and copy the exact terminal command for deeper work.
7. I can see whether guest-read and host-write GitHub credentials are present without the app retrieving or displaying either token.
8. I can run and track a cold backup later without being surprised that previously running VMs are temporarily stopped and then restarted.

Success criteria: workspace state appears within two seconds of opening the popover and converges within ten seconds while idle; explicit actions refresh immediately and never execute twice concurrently; background polling never starts a stopped workspace; metrics collection runs only for visible/running workspaces and averages below 0.5% host CPU during idle use; every failure preserves stderr, names the affected workspace, and offers a valid CLI fallback; no credential value, command environment, or sensitive backup content is stored or logged; all controls are keyboard accessible and expose VoiceOver labels beyond color; Stop All, Restart All, backup, and any future state-changing bulk action require clear confirmation; notifications are deduplicated and pressure alerts require a sustained threshold with hysteresis; every documented command is deliberately classified as menu, detail, or terminal-only.

Settings: launch at login; refresh interval with a conservative 10-second default and backoff on repeated failures; show/hide resource badges; per-workspace default port, scheme, favorite ports, and recent project paths; optional notifications for unexpected stops, failed actions, sustained CPU/memory/disk pressure, and long-running job completion; configurable thresholds and quiet hours; preferred terminal and editor detection; confirmation toggles only for reversible individual lifecycle actions, never for bulk or destructive actions. An optional global shortcut may toggle the popover but should be disabled by default; menu-local shortcuts can use Command-1/2/3 to select workspaces and Return to open the default action. No destructive action should receive a global shortcut.

Persistence: use UserDefaults for preferences and favorites, plus a small atomic Application Support cache for recent ports/projects, last successful backup, and bounded metric samples. Runtime state remains authoritative in MicroSandbox and cached state must be visibly marked stale. Reuse the existing macOS Keychain boundary indirectly through msw; never copy, persist, or synchronize GitHub tokens. Avoid a database in P0.

Notifications: default to action failures and unexpected transitions only. User-initiated start/stop success should stay silent; backup completion may notify because it is long-running. Threshold alerts should require several consecutive samples, issue one notification per incident, and clear only after recovery. Notification text should avoid tokens, raw logs, and sensitive repository paths.

Implementation prerequisite and extensibility: do not scrape the current human-oriented msw status output, which combines msb ps with port prose, or keep parsing JSON with shell substring matching as sandbox_running currently does. Add a versioned, read-only machine contract before the native UI: status --json, metrics --json --once, disk --json with an explicit no-start mode, github status --json, and capabilities --json. The app should invoke the executable directly with argument arrays, never through a shell, and use a typed command adapter whose metadata declares read-only/state-changing/destructive, confirmation policy, timeout, and whether a stopped VM may be started. A cancellable job layer can later support backup, checks, and tunnels without expanding the popover.

Roadmap: Phase 0 defines and tests the versioned JSON/read-only contract and action-safety metadata. Phase 1 ships the P0 menu bar and compact detail window, lifecycle serialization, launch actions, stale/error handling, accessibility, login setting, and direct CLI fallbacks. Phase 2 adds P1 diagnostics, repository inventory, GitHub presence, bounded logs, favorites, notifications, and supervised backup. Phase 3 adds opt-in history, managed tunnels, update awareness, App Intents, dynamic workspace discovery, and an extension registry; repository and credential mutation remain excluded unless separately threat-modeled.

Repository grounding and verification: reviewed README.md, docs/MSW-CHEATSHEET.md, docs/SETUP-GUIDE.md, docs/TEST-REPORT.md, config.sh, and the complete command dispatch and relevant implementations in bin/msw. Cross-checked lifecycle auto-start behavior, fixed hosts and published ports, resource ceilings, cold-backup restart semantics, restore behavior, Keychain isolation, quarantine handling, and the documented 46-scenario release coverage. No project-wide tests, formatters, or linters were run, as requested. The repository was left untouched; existing unrelated working-tree changes were not modified.","filesChanged":[]}
